intro: The fifth movement of Ravel’s Le Tombeau de Couperin is a minuet in G major with a musette, a dance over a bagpipe-like drone, as its middle section. When the minuet returns, Ravel combines the two dances at the keyboard.

sections.label: A · Minuet in G major
sections.mNote: An ornamented melody above a moving bass.

sections.label: B · Musette over a drone
sections.mNote: G minor, with held bass notes under moving chords.

sections.label: A′ · Minuet over musette chords
sections.mNote: The minuet returns above the musette’s chords.

sections.label: Coda · Melody over left-hand arpeggios
sections.mNote: Left-hand arpeggios continue, then the tempo slows to the close.

cues.title: Opening of the Menuet
cues.text: A turn ornaments the first note of the melody. The tune moves in three beats over an independent bass line. Ravel marked the G major opening pianissimo and Allegro moderato.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 20; Piano Practical Editions, bars 1–8, p. 34. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP560971-PMLP4975-Le_Tombeau_de_Couperin.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Jean Dreyfus
cues.text: The Menuet is dedicated to Jean Dreyfus, who was killed in the First World War. Ravel wrote to his stepmother, Madame Fernand Dreyfus, from the front. She later took him into the family home in Normandy, where he recovered from military service and worked on this suite.
cues.evidence: The dedication is recorded by the BnF: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb13917720k. Family relationship, wartime correspondence and Normandy stay: Eric T. Williams, Kansas City Symphony programme, 5–7 April 2024, pp. 5–6. https://www.kcsymphony.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/FY24-CS10-Program-Book-Digital-2024-04-05.pdf

cues.title: Composition, 1914–1917
cues.text: Ravel began in 1914 with a single piano Forlane. Military service interrupted the work, and he returned to it in the spring of 1917, after his discharge. He dedicated each piece to the memory of a friend or comrade killed in the war.
cues.evidence: Orchestre national de Lyon programme note by Coline Miallier (25 and 27 November 2021): the 1914 Forlane, the interruption by military service, the resumption in spring 1917 and the dedications to fallen comrades. https://www.auditorium-lyon.com/en/node/13646

cues.title: Musette, bars 33–48
cues.text: The central dance is a Musette. Its chords move over a drone, the keyboard’s imitation of a bagpipe. The tune uses B♭ and E♮, which places it in G Dorian, a minor mode with a raised sixth step.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, Musette; Piano Practical Editions, bars 33–48, p. 35. The edition’s commentary identifies G Dorian, a minor mode with a raised sixth.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Minuet and musette combined
cues.text: The minuet’s first melody returns in G major. Beneath it, the left hand plays the musette’s chords, so the two dances sound together.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 22; Piano Practical Editions, bars 73–80, p. 36, superimposes the minuet melody and musette accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano and orchestral premières, 1919–1920
cues.text: Marguerite Long gave the first performance of the piano suite at the Salle Gaveau on 11 April 1919. Ravel later scored four of its six movements for small orchestra, the Menuet among them. Rhené-Baton conducted them at the Concerts Pasdeloup on 28 February 1920.
cues.evidence: Orchestre national de Lyon programme note (2021): première of the piano version by Marguerite Long, Salle Gaveau, 11 April 1919; orchestration of four movements (Prélude, Forlane, Menuet, Rigaudon), first performed at the Concerts Pasdeloup on 28 February 1920 under Rhené-Baton. https://www.auditorium-lyon.com/en/node/13646

cues.title: Arpeggiated bass, bars 105–120
cues.text: The left hand changes from chords to arpeggios, and the melody rises above them as the hands move farther apart. Ravel writes one last broad phrase with a crescendo, then returns the piano to pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 23; Piano Practical Editions, bars 105–120, p. 38: arpeggiated bass, crescendo and the return to pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Silently depressed keys, final bars
cues.text: The closing page asks for much slowing, then Très lent. At the end Ravel told the pianist to press keys silently. The pedal clears, and only the notes whose dampers remain raised ring into the final G major chord.
cues.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, final bars; Piano Practical Editions, bars 124–128, p. 38, and commentary on bar 127: sans faire vibrer means to depress the keys silently.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From the Menuet to the Musette
transitions.how: The repeated strain of the minuet closes, and the piano begins the Musette softly. G remains the home note, and B♭ replaces B♮. Held bass notes support the moving chords. E♮ places the G minor dance in the Dorian mode. The bar stays in three beats.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), pp. 20–21; Piano Practical Editions, Menuet, bars 31–40, p. 35.

transitions.title: The minuet returns above the musette
transitions.how: The musette drops to pianissimo. The piano returns to G major and plays the opening melody of the minuet above the musette’s chordal accompaniment. The right hand keeps the minuet’s grace notes and long slurs. The left hand continues the steps of the middle dance.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 22; Piano Practical Editions, bars 65–80, p. 36.

transitions.title: Left-hand chords become arpeggios
transitions.how: The upper melody stays the same, and the left-hand chords are replaced by arpeggios. A gradual crescendo takes the hands farther apart across the keyboard. The line then falls back to pianissimo. Each of the following phrases is slower than the one before, and the movement closes in G major.
transitions.evidence: Durand piano score (1918), Menuet, p. 23; Piano Practical Editions, bars 105–128, p. 38.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
